source.title: MoE Sparsity Begets Monosemanticity: Insights into Understanding and Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Ming-Xue Tian; Qi Zhang; Xiao-Han Wang; Jia-Jun Chai; Guo-Jun Yin; Wei Lin; Cai-Lian Chen; Qi-Min Xu; Si-Yu Wang; Yi-Sen Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different framework and measure to test whether MoE activation sparsity is associated with expert-level monosemanticity, but it does not test feature superposition or its representational geometry.
record.gate_note: Fine-tuning benchmark comparisons do not measure the claim's representational object and are omitted. Evaluator-correlation results validate the scoring framework rather than test the claim. The study's reported sparsity–LDS result is retained as a related finding, not assigned to a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study measures how predictable each MoE expert's routing is from a GPT-4o explanation (EMS/LDS). It does not measure feature directions, superposition geometry, capacity competition, neuron-level polysemanticity rates or SAE features. Its sparsity result concerns routing top-k, not feature sparsity. It relates by analogy to SAE and superposition work but tests no version, so the reader's 'tests'/T2 is downgraded.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that MoE routing sparsity promotes expert-level monosemanticity, that middle layers are most specialized, and that experts are either domain-specific or general. They use this to motivate EDMRS expert-selective fine-tuning, which they report reduces forgetting. The record omits the middle-layer finding.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an expert-level explanation-and-activation-prediction framework and varies MoE top-k activation; it does not use the original toy-network feature-superposition method or measure feature-direction geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported monosemanticity varies with activation sparsity (k), network layer, and evaluated domain.

fits_no_version.finding: Lowering MoE routing sparsity (raising k at inference) lowers the mean explanation-predictability of experts (LDS) across four layers of Qwen3-30B-A3B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE LLMs, sparser expert routing is associated with more monosemantic (explanation-predictable) experts.

fits_no_version.finding: Domain-specialized and cross-domain experts coexist; EDMS is generally below EMS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE experts split into domain-specialized and shared experts.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert explanations are more abstract than explanations of the expert's own neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Experts encode coarser semantic units than their constituent neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3-235B-A22B, LDS rises in early layers, plateaus in the middle layers, and drops sharply near the output (Fig. 3b). No row records this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert monosemanticity in MoE LLMs peaks in middle layers.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
record.problems: The sparsity–LDS result is described qualitatively in the text and its numerical values are not stated. The study measures expert-level explanation-based monosemanticity, not feature overlap, representational capacity, or direction geometry.
record.rows_left_out: Fine-tuning results in Sections 5 and Appendix A.5–A.8 were omitted because they evaluate adaptation performance rather than the claim's representational object. Metric-reliability comparisons in Sections 3.1, 5.1, and A.9 were omitted because they validate the evaluator/scoring framework.

untested.parts: No toy models, no feature-vs-dimension setting, no geometry or phase transition.
No test of capacity competition or of dedicated vs shared dimensions by importance.
Expert-level cross-domain activation is not neuron polysemanticity, and no alternative cause is tested.
No measurement of features distributed across neurons, and no SAE or dictionary recovery.

record.verdict_notes: Monosemanticity here is the accuracy of GPT-4o predicting expert routing from an explanation. The sparsity manipulation changes inference-time k, not training, so it says nothing about how features are stored. The robustness checks (evaluator swap, Spearman 0.77–0.82; human agreement, 0.70) validate the metric only.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether limited representational capacity causes feature competition, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Reports shared/polysemantic experts, but does not test whether polysemanticity arises through a mechanism other than capacity pressure or whether it is evidence for superposition.
Does not measure features spread across neurons or features recovered by an SAE/dictionary.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not test whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of activated experts k to vary MoE sparsity and measured layer-wise decoupling score (LDS).
rows.measure: Layer-wise decoupling score (LDS), defined as average expert monosemanticity score (EMS) in a layer.
rows.value: The text reports that reducing sparsity consistently and substantially decreases LDS across all evaluated layers and k values; numerical LDS values are not stated.
rows.note: The text says the trend holds uniformly across evaluated k values, with no inflection near the pretraining default.
rows.check: Versions 'none' is correct. k is varied at inference on a model trained at a fixed k, so this is not a capacity or feature-sparsity manipulation. No numeric LDS values or k grid are given. The authors' claim that this rules out pretraining confounds is asserted, not shown. The state should not read as evidence for any version.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507
rows.operation_detail: Measured EMS and domain-specific EDMS for all 128 experts using general and domain-constrained explanation prompts.

conditions.value: multiple evaluated domains; specific set not stated here

rows.measure: Expert monosemanticity score (EMS) and expert domain monosemanticity score (EDMS).
rows.value: The text reports that EDMS scores are generally lower than EMS scores, and that domain-specialized and shared/polysemantic experts coexist; individual numerical scores are not stated.
rows.note: This is a reported pattern in expert-level domain specialization, not a measurement of superposed feature directions.
rows.check: Versions 'none' is correct. 'Polysemantic experts' are whole FFN modules activating across domains, not neurons or features, so this does not bear on V2 or V3. Only distributions are plotted (Fig. 4); no numbers are given.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Applied the monosemanticity evaluation framework separately to experts and neurons in a randomly selected intermediate layer.
rows.measure: Semantic granularity of generated expert and neuron explanations.
rows.baseline: expert explanations compared with neuron explanations
rows.value: The text reports that expert explanations operate at a higher, more abstract semantic level, while neuron explanations operate at a lower level.
rows.note: The comparison concerns explanation granularity, not the dimensionality of superposed features.
rows.check: The subject is not stated in A.10; it is presumably Qwen3-30B-A3B, since A.7 names it as the base model, but this is unconfirmed. The row is a qualitative case study of seven explanations (Table 8), not a polysemanticity measure.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
